venues.name: Lab
venues.note: On-campus / lab testing codes in forgiveness and cooperation files

sites.blurb: Greater Boston is the densest cluster of Mind & Culture Lab testing venues: preschool classrooms in Acton, park recruitment on Boston Common, Franklin Park Zoo outreach, and university labs at Boston College and related sites. Children here completed trust, forgiveness, inequity-aversion, and multi-task cooperation protocols with Boston-area collaborators.

sites.name: New Haven

venues.name: Yale-area schools and labs
venues.note: New Haven metro recruitment for risk/time and SSS studies

sites.blurb: New Haven provided the urban U.S. comparison samples for developmental risk and time-preference tasks and for MacArthur Ladder / Social Comparison Index ratings of subjective social status.

sites.name: Durham
sites.society: Toddler peers in lab and preschool settings
tasks: Key matching in dyads and triads
sites.blurb: Home of the Mind & Culture Lab at Duke. Same-aged two- and three-year-olds sat around a compact square table and coordinated magnetic keys on a square wooden box—in dyads (2 peers) and triads (3 peers)—at the lab and nearby schools.

sites.name: USA (urban)
tasks: Dice & opaque cup (epistemic vs physical uncertainty)
sites.sampleNote: Exact city is not named in the open EpistemicPhysicalDeid dataset; pin placed in the Northeast U.S. corridor near other lab comparison sites (offset from New Haven so both pins stay visible)

venues.name: Urban U.S. testing site (city not named in open data)

sites.blurb: One of three cultures in the epistemic-versus-physical uncertainty dice task (with Iran and Tsimané Bolivia). Participants chose Roll-Then-Guess versus Guess-Then-Roll after training with a six-sided die and inverted opaque cup. The de-identified open file codes this cohort only as USA.

sites.name: Antigonish / StFX
sites.society: Town and county communities around St. Francis Xavier University

venues.name: STFX Labs
venues.note: St. Francis Xavier University campus lab

venues.name: St. J’s / St J (town / CC / county)
Club 60 / 60 Town
venues.note: Town venue aliases in cooperation data

sites.blurb: Canadian testing centered on Antigonish and St. Francis Xavier University, with additional town and county venues (Arisaig, Heatherton, Club 60, Fun Skills, and related codes). Children completed both the four-task cooperation battery and the Inequity Game with reaction-time recording.

sites.name: Vadodara
sites.sampleNote: Primary open samples; separate India 1-week (N≈43) and 1-year ladder retest cohorts also archived
sites.blurb: Vadodara provided the Indian urban samples for risk and time-preference choices and for subjective social status (MacArthur Ladder + Social Comparison Index), including dedicated test–retest reliability waves.

sites.name: Srikakulam
sites.blurb: Coastal Andhra Pradesh site for the seven-society Inequity Game study. Children accepted or rejected fair and unfair candy allocations while reaction times informed drift-diffusion models of fairness.

sites.name: Iran (urban)
tasks: Dice & opaque cup (epistemic vs physical uncertainty)
sites.sampleNote: Open data codes country as Iran; pin placed at Tehran as a representative urban reference

venues.name: Urban Iranian communities (city not named in open data)

sites.blurb: The largest culture sample in the epistemic-versus-physical uncertainty paper (N = 100). Participants trained on a die under an opaque cup, then chose whether to roll before guessing (epistemic) or guess before rolling (physical).

sites.name: Tsimané
tasks: Dice & opaque cup (epistemic vs physical uncertainty)

venues.name: Tsimané communities along the Maniqui / nearby rivers

sites.blurb: Tsimané communities in lowland Bolivia—one of three cultures contrasting epistemic and physical uncertainty. Many participants had little or no prior exposure to dice, making this a critical test of whether uncertainty preferences depend on culturally familiar chance devices.

sites.name: Mayangna
sites.sampleNote: Archived in EpistemicPhysNicaraguaDeid.csv; not in the main explorer N = 210
sites.blurb: A supplementary Mayangna cohort from Nicaragua completed the same dice-task logic as the main three-culture sample. Materials live in the study’s local OSF files and analysis script for Nicaragua.

sites.name: Shuar — Upano Valley
sites.society: Shuar communities with greater market access (Upano Valley)

venues.name: Yamanunka
venues.note: Upano Valley in study2_data.csv; also cooperation battery

venues.name: Upano Valley (SSS / fullsample codes)
venues.note: MacArthur Ladder society code Upano Valley

sites.blurb: Upano Valley Shuar communities—closer to roads and markets than Cross-Cutucú—participated in cooperation games, risk and delay choices, and subjective social status ratings. Study 2 village codes place Yamanunka, Sintinis, and Pablo Sexo in the Upano Valley; San Pablo appears in the cooperation battery.

sites.name: Shuar — Cross-Cutucú
sites.region: Remote Amazonian Ecuador (east of the Cutucú range)

venues.name: Cross-Cutucú (SSS / fullsample codes)
venues.note: MacArthur Ladder society code Cross Cutucu

sites.blurb: Cross-Cutucú Shuar communities east of the Cutucú mountains provided the remote market-integration contrast for risk, time preference, and subjective social status. Study 2 places Panints and San Ramon in Cross-Cutucú (not Sintinis or Pablo Sexo, which are Upano Valley).

sites.name: San Pedro de Saño
sites.blurb: San Pedro de Saño in Peru contributed one of the largest non-U.S. samples: primary and high-school students in the cooperation battery, plus a large Inequity Game reaction-time cohort in the seven-society fairness study.

sites.name: Toba/Qom

venues.name: Toba/Qom communities in the Gran Chaco

sites.blurb: Toba/Qom communities in Argentina’s Gran Chaco completed the same risk and time-preference battery and MacArthur Ladder status measures used in India, Ecuador, and the U.S., enabling direct cross-society developmental comparisons.

sites.name: Maya communities
sites.society: Maya children (coded “Maya” in the seven-society dataset)
sites.sampleNote: Open data location code is simply “Maya”; pin placed in the Yucatán Maya region used in related Kramer / McAuliffe collaborations
sites.blurb: Maya children in Mexico formed one of the seven societies in the computational inequity-aversion study, contributing accept/reject decisions and reaction times for drift-diffusion modeling.

sites.name: Tooro / Kasiisi

venues.name: Kasiisi
venues.note: All cooperation Uganda sample + largest inequity venue

sites.blurb: Western Uganda testing around Kasiisi and neighboring village schools (Kigarama, Kiko, Kanyawara) near Fort Portal. Children completed both the four-task cooperation battery and the Inequity Game with reaction-time recording.

sites.name: Senegal (Dakar area)
sites.sampleNote: Pin nudged slightly inland of coastal Yoff so it sits on land in the globe texture (Dakar peninsula is a thin coastal strip at this map resolution)
sites.blurb: Senegalese children in Yoff, Boune, and Diacksao (Dakar area) contributed Inequity Game decisions and reaction times as one of the seven societies in the computational fairness paper.
